procedural_history.impugned_order: Non-consideration of interlocutory applications by DRT Bengaluru despite urgency and large amounts involved. Refusal of the High Court of Karnataka to pass any ad interim direction.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Petitioners-banks filed Writ Petition Nos. 12191-12194 of 2016 in the High Court of Karnataka seeking directions to DRT Bengaluru to hear and dispose of applications moved by the banks. The High Court refused to pass any ad interim direction.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The petitioners-banks filed Special Leave Petitions (SLP (C) Nos. 6828-6831 of 2016) in the Supreme Court after the High Court refused to pass any ad interim direction. The Supreme Court issued an interim order of injunction against Respondent Nos. 1 to 3 from transferring, alienating, disposing of, or creating third-party rights in respect of movable and immovable properties. The Supreme Court also issued notice in respect of I.A. Nos. 1 to 4 of 2016 seeking recall of the Order dated 25.07.2016.

directions: to freeze the passport of Respondent No.3

issue.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court can take cognizance of the violation of an order passed by the High Court, or should it be left to be decided by the High Court itself in a properly instituted legal proceeding.

facts: The respondent violated restraint orders that had been passed by the High Court.
The violation of the High Court's orders occurred in the "very same cause" (legal case) that was being dealt with by the Supreme Court.
The violation of the High Court's orders was also "coupled with the violation of orders of this Court as well."
The respondent was put on clear notice by the Supreme Court about the violation of the High Court's orders but failed to file a reply.
law: The Supreme Court, as the Apex Court, is the "protector and guardian of justice throughout the land."
The Supreme Court has a right and a duty to protect lower courts, whose orders are subject to its correction, from acts of contempt committed against them.
application: The Court reasoned that since it was already dealing with the same underlying legal case in which the High Court had passed its orders, it was appropriate for the Supreme Court to address the violation.
The fact that the respondent had also violated the Supreme Court's own orders further justified the Court's decision to handle the entire matter.

The Court dismissed the concern that the respondent would be prejudiced by losing an opportunity to have the matter heard by the High Court first. It noted that the respondent had been given clear notice of the alleged violation and an opportunity to respond, which they did not take, meaning no prejudice was caused.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that it can and ought to take cognizance of the violation of the High Court's order because it has a duty to protect lower courts from contempt, and because the violation was part of the same case and linked to violations of the Supreme Court's own orders.

issue.issue_text: Whether the application (I.A. Nos. 1 to 4 of 2016) to recall the order requiring Respondent No.3 to appear in person in the contempt proceedings should be allowed.

facts: Respondent No. 3 filed an application (I.A. Nos. 1 to 4 of 2016) seeking to recall a court order that had issued a notice for contempt proceedings against him.
In the same application, Respondent No. 3 also requested that his personal appearance in the contempt proceedings be dispensed with.
law: Under Rule 6(1) of the Rules to Regulate Proceeding for Contempt of Supreme Court, 1975, a person issued a notice in a contempt petition is obliged and duty-bound to appear in person.
application: The Court noted that instead of complying with his duty to appear in person as required by Rule 6(1), Respondent No. 3 chose to file an application to recall the notice.
The petitioners argued that this application was a "mere ruse to circumvent the law."
After considering the matter, the Court found "no reason to recall that order."
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court dismissed the application (I.A. Nos. 1 to 4 of 2016) and affirmed that Respondent No. 3 was duty-bound to appear in person for the contempt proceedings.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court can take cognizance of the violation of an order passed by the High Court, or should it be left to be decided by the High Court itself in a properly instituted legal proceeding.
appellant_arguments: The Supreme Court has the power to take cognizance of contempt of a subordinate court due to its supreme appellate jurisdiction over all courts and tribunals in the country.
respondent_arguments: While not seriously contesting the Supreme Court's jurisdiction, the respondent argued that if the jurisdiction is assumed, the matter should be left for the High Court to decide in a properly instituted legal proceeding.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the application (I.A. Nos. 1 to 4 of 2016) to recall the order requiring Respondent No.3 to appear in person in the contempt proceedings should be allowed.
appellant_arguments: The appellant's argument is not explicitly stated in the text, but as the opposing party to the recall application, their implied argument is that the order for personal appearance should be upheld and is necessary for the proceedings.
respondent_arguments: Respondent No. 3 filed an application to recall the court's order that required him to appear in person.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: An order of restraint governs all properties, whether movable or immovable, regardless of whether the properties were in the hands of the respondents on the date the order was passed or came into their hands or under their control at a later point in time.
obiter: The Supreme Court can and ought to deal with a violation of a High Court's order when it is dealing with the same cause of action and the violation is also coupled with a violation of the Supreme Court's own orders.
A respondent's submission that they would lose an opportunity of having the matter assessed at the level of the High Court if the Supreme Court assumes jurisdiction is a consideration for the court.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Supreme Court determined it has the jurisdiction and duty to take cognizance of contempt of a High Court's order. This is justified when the violation pertains to the very same cause of action being heard by the Supreme Court and is coupled with a violation of the Supreme Court's own orders. The Court's authority stems from its role as the apex judicial body responsible for protecting the integrity of all subordinate courts.
legal_tests_applied: The principle that the Supreme Court, as the Apex Court, is the "protector and guardian of justice throughout the land" and therefore has a right and duty to protect subordinate courts whose orders are amenable to its correction from acts of contempt.
policy_considerations: The Supreme Court has a systemic duty to protect the authority and dignity of subordinate courts to ensure justice is upheld throughout the country.

Assuming jurisdiction for a subordinate court's contempt does not cause prejudice to a party if they have already been put on clear notice of the alleged violation and the matter is part of the same cause being adjudicated by the Supreme Court.
